title: What should you ask first in a public sector case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a public sector case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first what success looks like, both for the people the service is meant to help and for the budget, because public sector goals are rarely profit and the case turns on which outcome matters most. The trap is forcing a profit lens onto a social goal, and missing who gains and who loses.
body:
The first question to ask

What does success look like for the people we serve, and what is the budget?

Governments, public services and charities pursue outcomes, usually several that pull against each other. A congestion charge aimed at cleaner air is designed differently from one aimed at raising money. So agree the main outcome, how it will be measured, and the budget or other constraints (political, legal, timing) before building anything.

How to build your structure

  • Stakeholders and objectives: who is affected, what each group wants, which outcome comes first.
  • Current performance: where things stand against targets, past years and comparable places.
  • Levers: policy and regulation, how the service is delivered, funding.
  • Implementation and risks: cost, public and political support, who could be left worse off.

The money tools still apply, but as means, not ends: compare options on outcome per dollar, not on profit. For many more prompts, see the public sector practice set.

A different objective changes the answer

A city wants to reduce overcrowding and long waits on its buses. A private operator might ask which routes make money. The city asks which spending cuts waiting time most, fairly, within a fixed budget.

Option A adds buses to one busy route for $1M a year. It cuts average waits by six minutes for 20,000 riders a day:

  • 20,000 × 6 minutes = 120,000 minutes, or 2,000 hours saved a day
  • Assume about 300 days of full service a year: 2,000 × 300 = 600,000 hours a year
  • Cost per hour saved: $1M ÷ 600,000 ≈ $1.67

Option B, a bus lane on another route, costs $600k a year and saves three minutes for 20,000 riders: 1,000 hours a day, or 300,000 a year, at $2.00 an hour. Option A is cheaper per hour saved, even though it costs more in total.

Then ask who benefits. If the busy route serves wealthier areas and an underserved neighbourhood relies on the route that would get the bus lane, the city may still choose B, or fund both by trimming elsewhere. The numbers frame the choice; the objective decides it. Say which trade-off you are making and how the city will measure whether it worked.

The trap most people fall into

Forcing a profit lens onto a social goal. "Cut the routes that lose money" may be right for a private operator and wrong for a city whose aim is access for people without cars.

Weak: "Route 12 loses the most money, so I'd cut its frequency and use the savings elsewhere."
Strong: "Our goal is shorter waits, fairly shared. Extra buses on Route 4 save time at about $1.67 an hour, against $2 for the bus lane. But Route 12 is the only link for two estates without good alternatives, so I'd protect it and fund Route 4 first."

Two prompts to try

Should a city introduce a congestion charge?

Show the answer
  • Objectives: less traffic, cleaner air, or revenue; alternatives such as parking charges, bus lanes, a low-emission zone.
  • Impact: drivers, residents, businesses, public transport users; who gains and who loses.
  • Economics: set-up and running costs; revenue and what it pays for.
  • Implementation: public and political support; technology, enforcement, timing.

Where to start: objectives. The right charge depends on whether the goal is traffic, air quality or revenue.

The trap: running straight to revenue without asking what the city wants to achieve.

A government wants 1 million more women in work within five years.

Show the answer
  • Who and where: which groups are out of work and why; regions and sectors with the biggest gap.
  • Barriers: childcare cost and availability; flexible hours, skills, transport.
  • Levers: childcare funding, tax and benefits; employer incentives, training.
  • Delivery: cost per extra woman in work; how to measure progress.

Where to start: who is out of work and why. The barriers differ by group, so split the group MECE first.

The trap: listing policies without first segmenting who is out of work.

Where to practise next

Try Kestrel Metro, free buses or more buses, and Riverside City, $10M to reduce homelessness. For choosing the right structure, see which framework fits which case.
